You don't really "agree" to an audit. If you get audited, you need to substantiate your income, deductions, credits, etc.

For very minor errors in paper filings, the IRS will often correct your taxes for you at no penalty (e.g. bad rounding where you end up off by a couple bucks +-).

For audits, penalties are fairly modest for inaccuracies (e.g. if you incorrectly took a $1000 deduction and were able to thereby decrease your taxes owed by $200, the IRS would likely charge you a penaltyin the 20-40% range, so you might pay $240-280 in taxes instead of the original $200). If you cooperate with an audit, the IRS is dramatically more likely to view any inaccuracies as "errors" (20-40% penalties) instead of:

Fraud. Fraud is where you can see jail time, 100% penalties, etc. e.g. if you fail to pay withholding taxes at all, dramatically mistate income (e.g. Al Capone claiming to have almost no income while maintaining a lavish lifestyle), or make blatantly false claims (like claiming deductions for 11 kids when you have zero children).

By govt agency standards, the IRS is one of most reasonable ones to deal with because they just want you to file your taxes in a timely and accurate fashion and to pay in a timely fashion. They're also very lightly staffed, so they don't have time to chase any but the most egregious offenders.
